title: What are you doing tomorrow? — the future
goal: Talk about plans — and avoid the mistake almost every learner makes: adding a second verb to *bom*. To say "I'll be at home", Slovenian needs nothing more than *bom doma*.
bekal: building the future: *bom* + the *-l* form of the verb
using *bom* on its own as the future of *biti*
recognizing that perfective verbs already point forward without *bom*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bom doma
dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon. Maja is making weekend plans, and Budi learns a rule that saves one word in every sentence.

notes: **Bom on its own already means "I will be".** This is the mistake learners most often bring over from English: *I will be at home* has two verbs, so people assume Slovenian does too. It doesn't. *Bom doma*, *Boš tam?*, *Bo lepo* — all complete. Adding *bil* is actually wrong.

**With other verbs, bom needs a partner ending in -l.** *Bom delal* (I'll work), *Bom kuhala* (I'll cook, female), *Bomo šli* (we'll go). The endings are exactly the same as the past-tense endings from unit 12 — so you'd mastered half of this system before the unit even started.

**Perfective verbs don't need bom at all.** *Gremo na Bled* already means "we'll go to Bled", *Skuham juho* means "the soup will be ready", *Ti povem jutri* means "I'll tell you tomorrow". This follows straight from the aspect you learned in unit 14: something finished can't be in progress, so it jumps forward by itself.

**Če bo lepo — "if" sentences use the future on both sides.** English uses the present after *if*; Slovenian doesn't bother and uses *bo*. *Če bo lepo, gremo* and *Če bo lepo, bomo šli* are both correct.

**The negative stands on its own: ne bom.** Unlike the past tense, which merges into *nisem*, the future writes *ne* separately: *Ne bom delal*, *Ne bo lepo*, *Ne bomo šli*. And since *ne bom* isn't a clitic, it can open a sentence.

grammars.title: Prihodnjik — the future tense
body: The forms of *bom*, plus the *-l* ending you already know from the past tense. Nothing here is really new except the helping verb.

after: Unlike *sem* in the past tense, **bom is not a clitic** — it can stand at the start of a sentence: *Bom delal* is correct, and so is *Delal bom*. The second puts slightly more stress on the work.

The *-l* ending follows exactly the same rules as in the past tense: *-l* one man, *-la* one woman or two men, *-li* two women or three or more, *-le* three or more women, *-lo* for things with no gender.

grammars.title: Three ways to point ahead
body: Slovenian has three roads to the future, and all three are used every day. What decides isn't grammar but feel.
after: The third way works just like English: "tomorrow I'm going to Maribor" uses the present and relies on the time word. Slovenian allows the same, so if *bom* isn't automatic yet, just name the time and carry on.

For a softer intention, use *bi rad* (would like): *Rad bi šel na Bled* (I'd like to go to Bled, male), *Rada bi šla* (female). It sounds polite and tentative, and it's very often used to suggest something without pushing.

blocks.text: Sentences for making, suggesting and canceling plans. Male forms; women add *-a* to words ending in *-l*.

blocks.text: *Bomo videli* — literally "we will see" — is used exactly like the English "we'll see": a polite, noncommittal answer that puts things off a little. Slovenians use it as often as English speakers do.

Notice *Ti povem jutri* too: the perfective verb *povedati* is used in the present, and *ti* sits in second place as a clitic. One short sentence using three different rules at once — a sign that you've reached the second half of this course.
Plans usually involve activities, so here are the ones Slovenians mention most when asked what they do in their free time.

To say you like doing something, use *rad* from unit 9 — and remember it agrees with the gender of the **speaker**: *Rad hodim v hribe* (male), *Rada hodim v hribe* (female), *Radi hodimo v hribe* (we).

**Hoditi v hribe** deserves special attention. Slovenia has more than ten thousand kilometers of marked hiking trails, and hiking is the true national sport — not just a weekend hobby. If someone invites you *v hribe*, the right answer is *Z veseljem!* and the right shoes.
